clue.text: Tempestuous, like Lady Georgiana's life

definitions.meaning: violent and turbulent, like rough weather
Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, led a famously turbulent, scandal-filled life

explanation.surface: A turbulent life story of an aristocratic lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean turbulent: weather that is wild, and a life full of quarrels and scandal like the Duchess of Devonshire's.

clue.text: Hidden themes in books about U-boats?

parts.note: a U-boat is a German submarine, a sub for short
books are texts

explanation.surface: A critic hunts for hidden meanings in naval war stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Books about U-boats would be 'sub texts', which read together give the word for underlying themes; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Underlying meanings that a work leaves unstated are what critics call its implicit layer.

clue.text: Gifts for Odette Swann, denied Miss Blandish

definitions.meaning: in Proust, Swann courts Odette with cattleyas, a kind of exotic flower
James Hadley Chase's thriller is titled No ... for Miss Blandish

explanation.surface: Flowers given to one literary heroine but withheld from another.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattleyas are tropical flowers of that family, Swann's love tokens, and Chase's title says Miss Blandish got none.

clue.text: Upset main Latin character in Nicholas Nickleby

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Latin scholar is disturbed by a figure in Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges MAIN and LATIN together into the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Mantalini is the affected, idle husband of the dressmaker Madame Mantalini in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Two months (one unsettled, one clear) to find Louisa M's youngest

indicators.note: one of the months is unsettled, its letters disturbed into a new order

parts.note: May is a month
March is another month

explanation.surface: A reader hunts through the calendar for a character from Little Women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one unsettled' turns MAY into AMY; the other month, 'one clear', stays as it is: MARCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Amy is the youngest of the four sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women.

clue.text: Notice physicist providing nom de plume for novelist

parts.note: to mark something is to notice it
Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who split the atom

explanation.surface: A scientist's name is borrowed as a writer's pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the pen name of the Victorian novelist William Hale White.

clue.text: Time's accompanies dance in roman veuve

definitions.text: Time's accompanies dance in roman veuve

parts.words: Time's accompanies dance in roman veuve
parts.note: Anthony Powell's twelve-novel sequence is A Dance to the ___ of Time, so the missing word goes with dance and time

explanation.surface: A French phrase about time and dance in a long novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roman veuve' stands where the term 'roman fleuve', a long novel sequence, is meant; Powell's sequence is the famous English example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word completes the title A Dance to the ___ of Time, Powell's sequence of novels.

clue.text: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)

definitions.text: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)

parts.words: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)
parts.note: the blank in Sassoon's poem Blighters names a syncopated popular dance music of the music halls

explanation.surface: A quotation from a war poet with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Blighters Sassoon imagines a tank lurching to the syncopated jazz-age tunes played in the music hall.

clue.text: American name, said to be composer

indicators.note: said to be signals that the word is heard, not seen, and sounds like the result

parts.note: handle is American slang for a name or nickname

explanation.surface: An American's name sounds like that of a famous composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said to be' means the slang word for a name, HANDLE, sounds like the composer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: George Frideric Handel was the German-born composer of Messiah.

clue.text: Character of 5 required then cue Frazier, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps means the letters could be arranged some other way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A character in a novel is cued by someone called Frazier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges THEN CUE FRAZIER; 5 is the cross-reference to the novelist Mark Rutherford, whose novel bears this heroine's name.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the title heroine of Mark Rutherford's 1893 novel.

clue.text: Cut short objection to mythical creature in ceremonial vessel

indicators.note: cut short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an objection is a but, as in no ifs or buts
a centaur is the half-man, half-horse of Greek myth

explanation.surface: An objection to a centaur figurehead on a ship of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut short' takes the last letter off the word for an objection. 'mythical creature in ceremonial vessel' reads like a figurehead on a ship, but the creature is part of the wordplay and the vessel is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the Doge of Venice's state barge, used for the yearly marriage of the city to the sea.

clue.text: Long narrative on Newton from French author

parts.note: a saga is a long story, often of a family
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: A long story about Isaac Newton by a French writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Françoise Sagan wrote the novel Bonjour Tristesse.

clue.text: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)

definitions.text: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)

parts.words: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)
parts.note: the blank in Frost's poem The Lesson for Today is the brief inscription on a gravestone

explanation.surface: A quotation from Robert Frost with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Frost's line ends with his own grave inscription: 'I had a lover's quarrel with the world'.

clue.text: Lie like Goya's Maja

definitions.meaning: lie as in lie back or lie down
Goya's paintings of the Maja show a woman stretched out on a couch

explanation.surface: Lying down in the pose of Goya's famous painted woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean back at rest is to lie, and Goya painted the Maja propped on cushions in just that pose.

annotationWithheld.clue: British composer is into its complications

clue.text: Instrumental passage from Little Dorrit or Nelly's Version

indicators.note: from tells the solver to take the letters out of the titles that follow

explanation.surface: A musical passage drawn from one of two novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to the run of letters across 'DorRIT OR NELly's'. Nelly's Version is a novel by Eva Figes.
explanation.definitionFit: A ritornello is a recurring instrumental refrain in a vocal work; this is the older English spelling.

clue.text: Mr Presley is not quite sure as stage manager

parts.note: Reg Presley was the singer of the Troggs; the surface wants Elvis

indicators.note: not quite right means the letters of the word are slightly disordered

explanation.surface: A rock singer is uncertain about becoming a theatre manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Presley' looks like Elvis, but it is Reg Presley of the 1960s band the Troggs. 'not quite' rearranges SURE into SEUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A régisseur is a stage director or ballet master, the person who runs productions in a theatre.

clue.text: A woman in love

parts.note: read as a reference to D. H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love, whose heroines are two sisters

explanation.surface: A lovestruck woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursula and Gudrun of that surname are the sisters at the centre of Lawrence's Women in Love.

clue.text: Gilbert's solitary game

definitions.meaning: a work by W. S. Gilbert, the comic opera written with Sullivan
a card game for one player, also called solitaire

explanation.surface: A man named Gilbert plays cards by himself.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera and the British name for card solitaire.

clue.text: The signs may well be grave, if not acute

definitions.text: The signs may well be grave, if not acute

parts.words: The signs may well be grave, if not acute
parts.note: grave and acute read as words for a serious illness, but they are the names of marks over letters

explanation.surface: A doctor warns that a patient's symptoms are serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave and acute are diacritic marks written over vowels, as in French.

clue.text: Greek always poetically describes feminist writer

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A classical poet's words are used to describe a feminist author.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine Greer wrote The Female Eunuch.

clue.text: It describes part of speech

parts.note: read as a grammar term, but it means a describing word or phrase attached to a name

explanation.surface: A definition from a grammar book.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive word or phrase added to a name, like 'the Great', is a term from rhetoric.

clue.text: He wrote 12 for a spy

parts.note: 12 refers to the entry at 12 across, which with 'for a spy' makes the title of a 1938 thriller

explanation.surface: Someone wrote twelve things for a secret agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Ambler wrote the spy novel Epitaph for a Spy.

clue.text: Avenging regicide of Fife

parts.note: the Thane of Fife in Shakespeare's Macbeth kills the king to avenge his murdered family

explanation.surface: A Scottish king-killer seeking revenge.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play the Thane of Fife slays Macbeth, who murdered his wife and children.

clue.text: A wave of the arms

parts.note: arms read as limbs, but they are a coat of arms, where wavy lines have a heraldic name

explanation.surface: Someone waves their arms.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the term describes a line drawn wavy across a shield.

clue.text: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets

definitions.text: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets

parts.words: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets
parts.note: winding sheets are shrouds, and Allingham's mystery is called The ___ in Shrouds

explanation.surface: A crime writer places a body in grave-clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Allingham's 1938 Campion mystery is titled The Fashion in Shrouds.

clue.text: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title

definitions.text: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title

parts.words: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title
parts.note: Anthony Powell's Books Do Furnish a Room: a room fitted with bookshelves has its walls covered

explanation.surface: A flat with shelving reminds someone of a novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Walls covered with bookshelves are said to be book-covered in this way, evoking Books Do Furnish a Room.

clue.text: Spectacle of new war heroes

indicators.note: new means the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A parade of fresh war heroes makes a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A raree-show was a peep show carried in a box by travelling showmen, hence any spectacle.

clue.text: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider

definitions.text: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider

parts.words: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider
parts.note: Laurie Lee wrote Cider with Rosie; put his subject's name with his own and the rhyming slang for tea results

explanation.surface: A writer and his muse prefer tea to cider.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosie Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, so swapping 'cider' for 'tea' in Laurie Lee's memoir Cider with Rosie gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang uses the name for a cup of tea, and Rosie is the girl in Lee's memoir.

clue.text: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"

definitions.text: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"

parts.words: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"
parts.note: from Wordsworth's sonnet The World Is Too Much With Us, naming the sea-god who blows a conch

explanation.surface: A poet describes someone blowing a horn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek sea-god, son of Poseidon, is shown blowing a conch shell to calm the waves.
